items.title: EU wants ‘closest possible relationship’ with UK after agreeing Brexit reset deal – live
items.summary:
President of European Council says EU ‘remains open to have the closest possible relationship’ with the UK

Senior correspondent

Making today’s reset deal contingent on a further agreement on the level of tuition fees for EU citizens is designed to neutralise the leverage London gets in the next six months, EU sources have said.

Senior diplomats had already confirmed this week that the EU would defer the deal on the level of tuition fees for another six months, a move designed to give the UK leverage in parallel negotiations to have the UK included in Made in Europe legislation designed to protect EU supply chains against China.

But the move to make the food and drink deal also contingent on a tuition fees deal effectively seeks to neutralise the leverage the UK gets today.

This is a serious chess game and shows the EU, again, is willing to speak very warmly about the UK but will play absolute hard ball when it comes to conceding any points to a former member state.

It was the same point France was making last night insisting the UK could not have voting rights on legislation in relation to food and drink.

During his meeting with businesses in Brussels, PM Burnham said his EU deal would add up to 0.5% to the UK’s GDP.

“We’re pretty much there, and it’s a really good deal.”

“Treasury analysis out today is saying that now it’s clear up to 0.5% on GDP as a result of the deal. The single biggest…

items.title: AT&T CEO says 200,000 fiber and telecommunications workers are needed thanks to AI—they’re stable, $70K-paying jobs that don’t require a degree
items.summary:
Data center development has become one of the largest contributors to U.S. economic growth , with roughly $800 billion expected to be spent in 2026 alone. But the AI-driven infrastructure boom is creating demand for a workforce that can build and connect those facilities—and the U.S. doesn’t have nearly enough workers to keep up.

According to AT&T CEO John Stankey , the shortage has become an increasingly urgent challenge. By 2032, he said the telecommunications industry will need to bring in nearly 200,000 additional construction and technician workers.

“We all know there’s a huge building boom going on, trying to bring the next foundational technology of AI out, and all those data centers have to be connected,” Stankey said on the This Old House Radio Hour podcast . “If we want to keep growing, we really need to address this and step up to it.”

On top of the rapid construction of data centers , the gradual expansion of broadband infrastructure to homes and businesses and the need to replace workers leaving through retirement and attrition is also putting strain on the industry—but it’s also presenting a newfound opportunity for Gen Z.

A shortage of telecom workers is an open door for Gen Z looking beyond a four-year degree 

With the college-to-career pipeline growing less reliable, the shortage of telecommunications technicians could offer young people a promising alternative to a four-year degree.

Most entry-level jobs in the space, including fiber technician, telecommunications installer, and construction jobs, don’t require a bachelor’s degree and offer paid,…
items.t: AT&T CEO says 200,000 fiber and telecommunications workers are needed thanks to AI—they’re stable, $70K-paying jobs that don’t require a degree

items.title: The FAA knew 51 of its 138 systems were unsustainable. Then it grounded every flight in America
items.summary:
In a span of 48 hours, Americans faced the full cost of slow-walking technology.

The Microsoft 365 outage on Nov. 12 – which knocked out email for companies nationwide – significantly slowed business operations across the global economy. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) decision to ground flights nationwide for nearly four hours on Nov. 13 led to thousands of flight cancellations and brought the economy to a halt.

While the two events are not technically related, they both demonstrate an off-balance sheet liability. In the classes I teach at Columbia Business School, which include chief financial officers, financial directors, and board members, I have characterized it as technical debt – the cost of hardware and software modernization that has not been done and keeps getting postponed. The problem for Americans: when companies and governments refuse to pay this technical debt, the results can be disastrous.

Businesses and governments alike are focused on short-term thinking – they’re incentivized to prepare for the next quarterly report or the next election. There are always pressing demands on funds today for other worthwhile and needed causes that offer near-term rewards. But I would go as far as to argue that technical debt is the biggest liability, and it doesn’t sit on any company’s balance sheet. This belongs almost to the same category of underfunded pensions and off-balance-sheet leases.

Framed in the language of finance, think of technical debt as unhedged, variable-rate operational debt. The upfront cost of the modernization not done is the…
items.t: The FAA knew 51 of its 138 systems were unsustainable. Then it grounded every flight in America

items.title: Ex-Super Micro executive, married to Jensen Huang’s ex-sales chief, says she took a CEO job at an Nvidia customer days before a $2.5 billion China smuggling scandal broke
items.summary:
A little-known figure in the palace intrigue involving Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and possible chip smuggling is rapidly gaining attention. Ying Cenly Chen, a former senior executive at Super Micro Computer , is alleged to have managed a significant portion of the company’s purchases of Nvidia chips during the period when Supermicro’s hardware was allegedly diverted to China, according to a lawsuit. Her new company, ChronoScale, where Chen serves as CEO, has business ties to both Supermicro and Nvidia. 

Chen matters because of her position at Supermicro and because of when she left. A shareholder lawsuit claims that Chen, 50, controlled Supermicro’s supply of Nvidia chips and could not have been unaware of the company’s alleged illicit sales. She exited Supermicro within weeks of an indictment that named Supermicro co-founder, Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw in the smuggling scheme. She is also married to Ajay “Jay” Puri, Nvidia’s longtime sales chief, Chen confirmed to Fortune . Puri worked for the chipmaker for two decades before announcing his retirement in June.

That means Chen could hold some answers to the question now looming large above Nvidia, which is whether Huang, who resigned as CEO on Nov. 11, knew or turned a blind eye as its chips were potentially diverted to China. And it puts a spotlight on her role at ChronoScale, which develops datacenters that rely heavily on Nvidia chips. 

Chen disputes the lawsuit’s account. In emails to Fortune , she said controlling customer allocations of Nvidia chips “was not part of my job responsibility” when she worked at Supermicro.…
items.t: Ex-Super Micro executive, married to Jensen Huang’s ex-sales chief, says she took a CEO job at an Nvidia customer days before a $2.5 billion China smuggling scandal broke

items.title: AI stocks are selling off after Anthropic’s record IPO, and Wall Street is split on whether this is the top
items.summary:
AI stocks are selling off again a day after Anthropic’s record IPO failed to steady them, and Wall Street is split on whether this is the top.

Anthropic priced its shares at $83 and closed its first day of trading Thursday at $97.17, up 17%, after raising $81.34 billion in the largest IPO ever, as Fortune ’s Shawn Tully reported . It wasn’t enough to keep the rest of the market from going the other way on Thursday. The Dow fell 1,101 points , or 2.19%, to 49,097, and closed below 50,000 for the first time since June. The S&P 500 fell 2% and the Nasdaq lost 2.2%.

The selling spread to Asia and Europe overnight, Fortune ’s Jim Edwards reported . Anthropic slid 11% on Friday, for a stock price around $86, while the Nasdaq lost 1.55% and the S&P 500 was down 0.5%.

The stakes go well past one stock. AI capital spending produced “about half” of S&P 500 earnings growth this year, according to Goldman Sachs Research, and Goldman’s equity strategists estimate the AI investment boom has lifted S&P 500 earnings 25% above trend. If you own an index fund, you own a bet on the data-center buildout.

The bear case 

James Reilly, senior markets economist at Capital Economics , wrote Friday that the falls in tech stocks and the S&P 500 “have further to run.” The success of Anthropic’s IPO as other AI-related stocks tumbled, he wrote, “highlights how different parts of the AI ecosystem no longer move as one.”

That split already shows up in prices. Since the S&P 500’s Oct. 6 record high, Nvidia is down 39% and Intel is down 50%. But investors still bought into Anthropic’s IPO at a $1.5…
items.t: AI stocks are selling off after Anthropic’s record IPO, and Wall Street is split on whether this is the top

items.title: ‘You either take the wheel, or we’re going to run into the wall’: The founder who sold Wrike for $2.25 billion forced his engineers to build around AI
items.summary:
Andrew Filev wanted his engineers to move three times faster, so he built a machine they couldn’t keep up with.

He set up what he calls a “human-AI factory.” Agents churned out code changes—pull requests, or PRs, in engineering terms—far faster than his team had ever handled, with one rule attached: an engineer had to review every one of them the same day. The old way of working couldn’t clear that bar. 

“Imagine I put them in a car, I gave myself a pedal and I floored it,” the Wrike founder told Fortune . “And I’m like, you either take the wheel, or we’re going to run into the wall. It’s your choice, but I was still flooring it.” He didn’t pretend it would be easy, either. “I was transparent about it,” he said. “I understand your way is not going to work. So don’t come to me and say it’s impossible.”

Filev has some standing to run this experiment. He built Wrike, one of the original collaborative work management platforms, which Citrix bought for $2.25 billion in 2021 . After Wrike, he founded For Good AI and spent a couple of years building its AI coding agent, Zencoder. Now he’s taking those engineers into a new product, Hops, an AI workspace for whole teams that opened to the public on Nov. 10 after more than 2,500 teams tried it in early access. It has $35 million in funding, Fortune can exclusively reveal. About two-thirds of that is Filev’s own money; the rest came from a handful of angel investors.

The experiment Filev ran on his new company speaks to the problem Fortune 500 executives keep running into this year: Their people are getting faster with AI, and…
items.t: ‘You either take the wheel, or we’re going to run into the wall’: The founder who sold Wrike for $2.25 billion forced his engineers to build around AI

items.title: Someone did the math on the Democrats’ first 100-day agenda: It saves $30 billion on the Iran war but adds $4.1 trillion to the national debt
items.summary:
While it’s the responsibility of the Department of the Treasury to finance the interest on the U.S.’s $40 trillion national debt, it is members of both parties in Congress who have added to Uncle Sam’s borrowing.

With the Democrats winning a wave of seats in the midterm elections, everyone from Wall Street analysts to CEOs of America’s largest companies are wondering what a more divided government will mean.

Budget watchdogs are doing the same, and the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) has put a number on how much the Democrats’ plan for their first 100 days will cost.

The Democrats will go into the 120th Congress with slim majorities in both chambers, and they have been clear about what they want to achieve in their first three months with more power. Hakeem Jeffries, nominated by Democrats to be the Speaker of the House of Representatives, wrote in November that the first 100-day agenda comprises “reverse the Medicaid cuts, restore SNAP funding, extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits, eradicate the Trump tariffs, and stop the reckless war of choice in Iran.”

Some factors come with obvious budget implications: De-escalating the war in the Middle East would save money, while ending Trump tariffs would axe a revenue stream that generated $287 billion in customs duties, taxes, and fees in 2025 per the Richmond Fed—up 192% on the prior year. 

The CRFB estimates that, in total, the “First 100 Days” policies would cost $4.1 trillion through 2037. Without offsets (spending cuts or revenue increases used to balance new policies), $4.9 trillion would be…
items.t: Someone did the math on the Democrats’ first 100-day agenda: It saves $30 billion on the Iran war but adds $4.1 trillion to the national debt

items.title: Intuit moves to sell Mailchimp for $3.68 billion as AI reshapes its growth strategy
items.summary:
Good morning. Intuit is unwinding its biggest acquisition while betting AI can help it win customers without owning the marketing platform it once viewed as central to that effort.

The QuickBooks and TurboTax parent announced Thursday it plans to sell Mailchimp, an email marketing automation platform, to Bending Spoons for approximately $3.68 billion. The deal is expected to close in early 2027, subject to approval, with proceeds earmarked for fiscal 2027 share repurchases. Intuit paid approximately $12 billion for Mailchimp in 2021. Mailchimp’s quarterly revenue fell 1% to $313 million.

Sasan Goodarzi, CEO of Intuit ( No. 231 on the Fortune 500) said on the earnings call that Intuit still wants to help businesses manage lead-to-cash needs, but believes it can do so more effectively by building AI-powered capabilities into QuickBooks rather than owning Mailchimp.

Mailchimp sale marks strategic shift 

The divestiture adds another dimension to what CFO Sandeep Aujla has called Intuit’s “reset to reaccelerate” strategy launched in August: accepting some near-term pressure on revenue per customer to rebuild customer acquisition. The strategy includes lower upfront revenue per TurboTax customer as Intuit seeks faster customer growth.

The latest results offered evidence of operating momentum. For the fiscal first quarter ended Oct. 31, revenue rose 12% to $4.35 billion, while adjusted earnings per share increased 56% to $2.91. Both exceeded analyst expectations.

In my conversation with Aujla, he pointed to mid-market revenue growth of 41% and customer growth of 30% as…
items.t: Intuit moves to sell Mailchimp for $3.68 billion as AI reshapes its growth strategy

items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
items.summary:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

items.t: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers

items.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
items.summary:
Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism

It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

Continue reading...
items.t: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier

items.title: Anthropic’s IPO is a bellwether—and a warning
items.summary:
In today’s CEO Daily: Is the creator of Claude worth it? 

The big leadership story: A tariff refund boosts Target’s profits. 

The markets: Down globally as Anthropic’s debut fails to improve market sentiment. 

Plus: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune . 

Good morning. Anthropic just pulled off a record-breaking IPO , with the five-year-old company debuting at a value of $2 trillion. Is the creator of the Claude chatbot worth it? Will customers get enough value from its products to pay prices that justify that valuation? Is confidence in AI moving faster than companies’ ability to capitalize on it? After all, there are two ways to vote on AI: Buy the stock or buy the product. The first tells us how much capital investors are willing to commit. The second tells us whether customers get enough value to keep paying.

There are plenty of data points to discuss. Start with the org chart, which is the opposite of founder mode: CEO Dario Amodei has one direct report (Jensen Huang had 60 at Nvidia), with most of Anthropic’s senior team reporting to his sister, President Daniela Amodei. The average Anthropic employee is now worth more than $40 million . (Daniela, lunch is on you.) Anthropic’s novella-length list of risk factors about its products still reads like a dystopian sci-fi thriller . The company’s ownership structure, from the role of the Long-Term Benefit Trust to the Class F shares, can warm your heart and hurt your head. Who will decide when to speed up or slow down? 

For now, let’s look at this debut as both a bellwether of current AI sentiment and a…
items.t: Anthropic’s IPO is a bellwether—and a warning

items.title: From losing it all to a $1 billion valuation: How Motorway’s CEO bounced back from failure
items.summary:
Tom Leathes and his two friends, Harry Jones and Alex Buttle were on a winning streak. Together, they built and sold office space platform Officila Space, broadband comparison site Top10.com, and LoanCube, a lead-generation site that was sold for $1 million. 

“We had this run of successes and thought we could do no wrong,” Leathes told Fortune. “And then we got quite schooled.” 

Their next business, a hotel recommendation app that kept the Top10 name, was their first to raise venture capital. It grew quickly, until Booking .com and the big hotel chains caught developed their own mobile apps. “All of the big hotel brands got mobile and killed us,” Leathes said. 

The founders spent two years trying to rescue the business, and a sale fell through at the last minute. They shut it down in 2015. “We lost all the money for the investors,” he said, referring to the $12.4 million the company had raised from backers including Balderton Capital and Accel. “We had to let go of the whole team.” The startup had 14 employees in London when it raised its last round in 2014. 

It was a “tough lesson,” Leathes admitted. The three went their separate ways, but within six months they were back together. “We had unfinished business,” he said. Their next venture, the trio agreed, had to be “the big one—the company that we can do for the next 10 or 20 years.” 

Leathes, Jones, and Buttle set about developing their next business idea from a disused hospital in Camden, north London, that was scheduled to be demolished. A charity had taken over the lease and was renting out the abandoned wards…
items.t: From losing it all to a $1 billion valuation: How Motorway’s CEO bounced back from failure

items.title: The Altruists review – two of TV’s best actors light up this chaotic crypto tale
items.summary:
Julia Garner and Anthony Boyle play the FTX founders behind ‘the greatest fraud ever committed’ in the US. It’s a mind-boggling story – just make sure you don’t miss a single moment

What happens when you put really stupid clever people in charge of the world? Not as presidents (they currently trend mostly towards the merely stupid) or prime ministers (generally neither really stupid nor really clever), but in charge of the real world, which is to say the online world, the one that really governs us? We are watching that play out day by day, but if you have enough slack left in your dread-system, a cortisol spike yet to execute, why not add a warning from history to your consumption of horrors?

Welcome to The Altruists, a breakneck breakdown of the brief career of Sam Bankman-Fried (played by Anthony Boyle) who, with his on-off girlfriend Caroline Ellison (played by Julia Garner), set up the cryptocurrency exchange FTX with the belief that it would revolutionise finance and – as the increasingly absurd/dishonest/knowingly satirical Silicon Valley mantra has it – make the world a better place. A very few years later, FTX – worth $36bn (£27bn) at its peak – collapsed and in 2023 the pair were convicted of various charges deriving from what the trial judge called “the greatest financial fraud ever perpetrated in this country”. Ellison was sentenced to two years in prison after testifying against Bankman-Fried. Bankman-Fried is serving 25 years and was ordered to forfeit $11bn (£8.3bn). He says he is innocent and is applying to the supreme court to review his…
